claims.text: The starting material is HfZrTiTa0.53 refractory high-entropy alloy.
The untreated alloy has a quasi-static yield strength of 786 MPa.
The untreated alloy has a quasi-static compressive strength of 1314 MPa.
The untreated alloy has a quasi-static fracture strain of 13.5%.
A minor Nb addition combined with controlled aging will induce uniformly distributed nanoscale precipitates in HfZrTiTa0.53.
The induced nanoprecipitates will pin dislocations.
Dislocation pinning by the nanoprecipitates will increase work hardening.
The nanoprecipitates will delay shear localization during high-strain-rate compression.
The nanoprecipitates will enhance dynamic recovery.
The treatment will moderately increase dynamic yield strength relative to the untreated alloy.
The treatment will increase dynamic compressive strength relative to the untreated alloy.
The treatment will improve uniform plastic deformation and delay strain localization.
The treatment will increase fracture strain under high-strain-rate loading.
The treatment will improve impact-energy absorption and resistance to rapid failure.
The predicted effects apply under adiabatic compressive loading at strain rates from 10^3 to 10^4 s^-1.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis describes enhanced 'impact-induced energy release' as equivalent to improved energy absorption. Energy release and energy absorption are distinct and potentially opposing outcomes, so the intended prediction is ambiguous.

The stated numerical baseline is quasi-static, whereas the predicted strength and ductility changes are dynamic. Directly describing dynamic changes relative to those quasi-static values is not a matched comparison, although the proposed experiment later includes a dynamic untreated control.
